claims.text: Solution treatment and water quenching produce a single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn single crystal with a dislocation density below 10^10 m^-2.
Yielding begins through thermally activated dislocation nucleation from pre-existing surface defects and Frank-Read sources.
A phase transformation is not the dominant mechanism for the onset of yielding.
The low Peierls stress of the FCC lattice permits dislocation glide with little thermal assistance at low strain rates.
At high strain rates, lattice-distortion obstacles delay the transition to athermal dislocation motion and require substantial stress to overcome.
The delayed transition to athermal motion creates a plateau in strain-rate sensitivity.
Lattice distortion strengthening and stacking-fault-energy variations control cross-slip and twinning and constitute the primary barriers to dislocation motion.
At higher stresses, interaction with the chemically disordered lattice through solute drag becomes rate-limiting rather than the Peierls barrier.
Collective unlocking of dislocation sources is the operative mechanism in FeNiCrMn.
Crystal-orientation anisotropy determines the critical resolved shear stress through the Schmid factor.
Crystals loaded along <111> have the highest yield strength, whereas crystals loaded along <100> have the lowest.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent will be approximately 0.01–0.03.
Yield strength will increase as temperature decreases from 600 K to 77 K.
The low-temperature increase in yield strength is caused by reduced thermal vibration aiding dislocation motion.
The temperature-dependent increase in yield strength will be smaller than in BCC alloys.
BCC metals exhibit strong strain-rate and temperature dependence because of screw-dislocation mobility.
The mild-to-wild plastic transition in BCC niobium is governed by athermal screw-dislocation slip.
If FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode, BCC diffraction peaks such as {110}BCC must emerge and grow concurrently with yielding.
The transformation hypothesis is falsified if the BCC fraction remains below 1% while the specimen yields and work-hardens.
Uncertain stacking-fault energy could permit TWIP or TRIP at cryogenic temperatures and alter strain-rate sensitivity.
